headline: Electronic skin gives robots a sense of touch

sources.title: Electronic skin gives robots and prosthetics human-like touch sensing (Robotics and Automation News)
Electronic skin enables tunable touch and proximity sensing (TechXplore)
Hanyang University researchers develop electronic skin with human-like touch (PR Newswire)
Electronic skin could give robots a sense of touch (video, BBC News)

chunks.text: Your skin can feel a [[raindrop]], a [[handshake]], or a hot cup before you even think about it. Robots cannot. Now [[researchers]] at Hanyang University in South Korea have built an electronic skin that can {{pick up}} even a very light touch. The results {{came out}} this year in the science [[journal]] Nano Energy. One day, the [[technology]] could {{give back}} a real [[sense of touch]] to people who use [[artificial]] hands.

verbs.why: A microphone can pick up the softest whisper, and a security camera can pick up motion in the dark. This new electronic skin can pick up even a very light touch, almost like real human skin.

verbs.correct: To be published for the public
verbs.wrong: To be tested in a hidden lab
verbs.why: A new study comes out in a science journal every month, and a popular book sometimes comes out years after the research began. The results of this project came out this year in the journal Nano Energy.

verbs.correct: To return something that was lost
verbs.why: A kind stranger might give back a lost wallet, and a doctor can give back movement to an injured arm. One day, this skin could give back a real sense of touch to people who use artificial hands.

chunks.text: The skin is a thin, soft [[layer]] with tiny electronic [[sensors]] inside. It feels [[pressure]], and it can even notice a finger that only [[comes near]] the [[surface]], before any [[contact]] happens. The clever part is that [[engineers]] can {{turn up}} its [[sensitivity]] with a small electric [[signal]], the way you raise the [[volume]] on a speaker. A soft version could be {{built into}} a robot hand, so the hand knows the difference between an egg and a rock.

verbs.why: You turn up the volume on a speaker, and you turn up the heat on a stove to cook faster. Engineers can turn up this skin's sensitivity with a small electric signal, the same way you raise a volume knob.

verbs.correct: To make something part of a machine
verbs.wrong: To place something on a shelf
verbs.why: Car makers build airbags into every new vehicle, and phone makers build a camera into the back of each phone. A soft version of this electronic skin could be built into a robot hand within a few years.

chunks.text: The team also tested how long the skin lasts. It {{went through}} more than one thousand touch tests and kept working without {{wearing out}}. It [[reacts]] in about one tenth of a second, almost as fast as human skin. The researchers {{hooked up}} a small square of one hundred sensors to a computer, and it could tell exactly where each touch [[landed]].

verbs.why: New cars go through crash testing before they reach a showroom, and new medicine goes through years of trials. This electronic skin went through more than one thousand touch tests and kept working the whole time.

verbs.correct: To stop working from long use
verbs.why: Old shoes wear out after months of daily walking, and a phone battery wears out after a few years of charging. In the tests, this electronic skin kept working for over a thousand touches without wearing out.
A technician might hook up new speakers to a stereo, and a nurse might hook up a monitor to a patient. Researchers in this study hooked up a small square of one hundred sensors to a computer.

chunks.text: There is still work to do. The scientists are {{figuring out}} how to cover a whole robot arm instead of one small [[patch]], and how to keep the skin cheap. But the [[direction]] is clear. If the technology {{takes off}}, future robots could help [[nurses]] lift [[patients]] gently, and an artificial hand could feel a child's [[grip]]. For machines, touch is no longer [[science fiction]].

verbs.correct: To find the answer to a problem
verbs.wrong: To write the results of a test
verbs.why: A driver might figure out a shortcut after a few wrong turns, and an engineer might figure out why a machine keeps failing. Scientists are still figuring out how to cover a whole robot arm instead of just one small patch.

A small business can take off after one good review, and a new song can take off on social media in a week. If this technology takes off, future robots could help nurses lift patients gently and safely.

mainIdea.s: Scientists in South Korea built an electronic skin that lets machines feel touch and nearby objects. It could improve robots and give artificial hands real feeling.
mainIdea.why: The Hanyang team's skin picks up light touch and close objects, and its sensitivity can be turned up with a small signal.

mainIdea.s: A research team taught a robot to feel real pain so it stops working when damaged. Korean factories will use the crying machines to warn workers about danger.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the skin senses touch and pressure, not pain. Nothing in the article says robots cry or stop working.

mainIdea.s: A hospital in South Korea replaced its nurses with soft robot arms this spring. Patients say the machines lift them more gently than human workers ever could.
mainIdea.why: The article is about a new sensing material in a lab, not about robots replacing nurses in a hospital.

lines.text: Researchers in South Korea built an electronic skin that can feel a touch lighter than a raindrop.

For robots, and maybe for people. It's a thin, soft layer with tiny sensors that {{pick up}} even the lightest pressure. It can even notice a finger that only comes near the surface, before any contact.
That's the clever part: engineers can {{turn up}} its sensitivity with a small electric signal, like raising the volume on a speaker.
Is it strong enough for real use?

It {{went through}} more than a thousand touch tests without {{wearing out}}, and it reacts in about a tenth of a second, almost as fast as human skin. The team {{hooked up}} a hundred sensors to a computer, and it could tell exactly where each touch landed.
What would robots do with it?
A soft version could be {{built into}} a robot hand, so it knows the difference between an egg and a rock. Future robots could help nurses lift patients gently.
[[That's the part that gets me]]. The technology could {{give back}} a real sense of touch to people who use artificial hands. Imagine feeling a child's grip again.
The results {{came out}} in the journal Nano Energy this year. The team is still {{figuring out}} how to cover a whole arm and keep it cheap.
Then touch stops being science fiction for machines.
Machines that feel. [[What a time to be alive]].
